subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Language Development, Bilingualism and Sign Language

subjective.question: What is the scope of psycholinguistics?
subjective.answer: Psycholinguistics is concerned with the relationship between the human mind and language. It is interested in the ways of storing lexical items and syntactic rules in the mind, and in the processes of memory involved in the perception and interpretation of texts. It is part of the emerging field of cognitive science and is principally an integration of the fields of psychology and linguistics.

subjective.question: What are the three main areas of psycholinguistics described by Clark and Clark?
subjective.answer: According to Clark and Clark, psycholinguistics covers three main points: (1) Comprehension — how people understand spoken and written language; (2) Speech production — how people produce language: spoken words are selected to be produced, their phonetics are formulated, and they are finally articulated by the motor system in the vocal apparatus; (3) Language acquisition — how people learn language.

subjective.question: Name the three pioneers who worked in psycholinguistics in the 19th century.
subjective.answer: 1) Paul Broca, 2) Charles Hockett, 3) Willem Levelt.

subjective.question: Name the three types of psycholinguistics.
subjective.answer: 1) Developmental psycholinguistics, 2) Social psycholinguistics, 3) Applied psycholinguistics.

subjective.question: What three questions did Chomsky present in his theory?
subjective.answer: 1) What constitutes knowledge of language? 2) How is knowledge of language acquired? 3) How is knowledge of language put to use?

subjective.question: Write a note on transformational (generative) grammar.
subjective.answer: Transformational grammar was an influential theory of grammar formulated by Chomsky in the late 1950s (Chomsky, 1957, 1965). Generative grammar regards grammar as a system of rules that generates exactly those combinations of words that form grammatical sentences in a given language. From a linguistic perspective, a grammar is a description of a person's linguistic knowledge — a formal device with a finite set of rules that generates the sentences in the language.

subjective.question: What are the three stages of development of the processing system?
subjective.answer: Stage 1: Input — the brain is exposed to a stimulus, at which point it analyzes and evaluates the information. Stage 2: Storage — our brains store the information for later use; the brain also adds it to our mental schema and encodes it. If the information is not reinforced, the brain may simply forget it over time. Stage 3: Output — the brain decides what it is going to do with the information and how it will react to the stimulus.

subjective.question: Explain the information-processing system.
subjective.answer: The general strategies by which the human mind encodes, stores, and retrieves information can be described independently of language. Working memory provides a temporary repository of information relevant for ongoing cognitive tasks; it is divided into three components: the central executive, the phonological loop, and the visuospatial sketchpad. Long-term memory is divided into semantic memory and episodic memory: semantic memory holds general knowledge, whereas episodic memory stores our experience from our personal perspective. Studies of individuals with various forms of brain damage suggest that these memory systems are controlled by distinct regions of the brain.

subjective.question: Define working memory.
subjective.answer: Working memory is only able to hold about seven units of information. This could simply be seven words, but because many sentences are longer than this, we need some way to deal immediately with more than seven words. One way we do this is to chunk the words into grammatical constituents such as noun and verb phrases, thereby reducing the storage burden to perhaps two or three constituents. The processing function of working memory is used to organize the words into the constituents.

subjective.question: Define long-term memory. What are its two types?
subjective.answer: Long-term memory is a memory structure that holds permanent knowledge. Tulving suggests that we should distinguish between two aspects of long-term memory: episodic memory and semantic memory. Episodic memory deals with personally experienced facts, while semantic memory deals with general facts. For example, knowing that John Wilkes Booth killed Abraham Lincoln is part of our semantic memory, but remembering when and where you first learned this information is a small part of your episodic memory.

subjective.question: Define episodic memory.
subjective.answer: Episodic memory stores our experience from our personal perspective. Studies of individuals with various forms of brain damage suggest that the episodic and semantic memory systems are controlled by distinct regions in the brain.

subjective.question: Explain memory for sentences.
subjective.answer: Memory is the process of retaining information over time. What we remember after one exposure to a single sentence is a mixture of the meaning of the sentence, its wording, and the inferences we draw at the time of comprehension. Numerous studies show that meaning predominates in our retention of sentences.

subjective.question: Explain working memory with respect to comprehension.
subjective.answer: Given the complexity of comprehension, working memory capacity is related to individual differences in comprehension performance. Gernsbacher and Faust provide evidence for this claim: they found that less skilled comprehenders were less efficient in rejecting the inappropriate meanings of ambiguous words. For example, when presented with a sentence such as 'He dug with the spade', less skilled comprehenders were slower to reject the meaning of spade that pertains to playing cards in favor of the meaning that pertains to gardening.

subjective.question: What do you understand by the term 'proposition'?
subjective.answer: A proposition is an idea unit; it is a statement that expresses a factual claim; it is the basic unit involved in the understanding and retention of text. Propositions correspond roughly to verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, and subordinating conjunctions (not nouns or pronouns).

subjective.question: Explain propositional representation briefly.
subjective.answer: Evidence for the psychological reality of propositions comes from Kintsch and Keenan, who showed that the number of propositions influences the time required to read a passage when preparing to recall it. Two sentences may have about the same number of words, yet the one with more propositions takes longer to read — Kintsch and Keenan found that each added proposition added about 1.5 seconds to the reading time. Later studies support the general conclusion that the number of propositions is related to reading time, and further work explored the notion that discourse is stored as a network of propositions.

subjective.question: What is proposition density? Why is it important in reading comprehension?
subjective.answer: Proposition density is an important factor in reading comprehension because of a proposition's role in text comprehension and retention. In addition, sentences in print often have a complex, embedded syntax that places demands on the reader's working memory.

subjective.question: Write a note on the hierarchical network model.
subjective.answer: A semantic network is an interconnected web of concepts connected by various relations. In the hierarchical network model, we store our knowledge of words in the form of a semantic network, with some words represented at higher nodes in the network than others. Although the hierarchical network model can explain some results, it is too rigid to capture all of our tacit knowledge of the lexicon.

subjective.question: What are semantic networks? Write the names of any three subtypes of semantic networks.
subjective.answer: A semantic network (or net) is a graphic notation for representing knowledge in patterns of interconnected nodes and arcs. Three subtypes are: 1) Implicational networks, which use implication as the primary relation for connecting nodes and may represent patterns of beliefs, causality, or inferences; 2) Executable networks, which include some mechanism, such as marker passing or attached procedures, that can perform inferences, pass messages, or search for patterns and associations; 3) Learning networks, which build or extend their representations by acquiring knowledge from examples.

subjective.question: What is lexical access? Which factors influence it?
subjective.answer: Lexical access is the process by which we retrieve words from the lexicon. It is influenced by a variety of factors, including the frequency of a word, its phonological structure, its syntactic category, its morphological structure, the presence of semantically related words, and the existence of alternative meanings of the word. Common words and meanings appear to be in a state of greater readiness than less-often-used words and meanings, and we rely on morphological structure when encountering unfamiliar words.

subjective.question: Write a note on two factors of lexical access: lexical frequency and word concreteness.
subjective.answer: Lexical frequency: in visual and auditory modalities, the more frequently a lexical item is used, the more quickly it is recognized. Word concreteness and imagery: words such as camera and banana are easy to imagine in our mind, whereas words such as justice and evil are more difficult to mentally picture. Word concreteness (also known as imageability) is the ability to visualize lexical items; concrete words are those that describe tangible nouns.

subjective.question: What is lexical ambiguity?
subjective.answer: The form of ambiguity in which a single word may be interpreted to have more than one meaning is referred to as lexical ambiguity. Foss was the first to apply the phoneme-monitoring technique to the study of lexical ambiguity, presenting listeners with sentences containing ambiguous words, such as: 'The man started to drill before the truck arrived.'

subjective.question: What is syntactic knowledge?
subjective.answer: Syntactic knowledge is our knowledge of the syntactic category, or part of speech, to which words belong. Two words belong to the same syntactic category when they can substitute for one another in a sentence. For example, in 'The aging pianist stunned the audience', we can replace aging with wealthy, poor, fat, or solemn, and although the substitutions may change the meaning of the sentence, the sentence remains grammatical. One advantage of using syntactic categories is that we can formulate grammatical rules in terms of categories rather than lexical items.

subjective.question: Define morphology and phrase structure.
subjective.answer: Morphology is the study of the structure of words: words consist of one or more units of meaning called morphemes, and the system of grammatical morphemes in a language provides speakers with a way of signaling subtle differences in meaning. Phrase structure refers to the grouping of words in a sentence: phrase-structure rules codify our intuitions about these groupings, and one type of phrase-structure rule — recursion — is responsible for the fact that there is no limit to the number of sentences in a language (linguistic productivity).

subjective.question: Differentiate between the modular and interactive models of parsing.
subjective.answer: The modular approach suggests that the words of a sentence activate syntactic processing strategies that are used to organize the words into a phrase marker. These strategies indicate that we prefer to attach incoming words to the most recent constituent rather than to earlier constituents or to developing new ones; although generally useful, they sometimes lead to errors and subsequent re-analyses of syntactic structure. The interactive approach emphasizes that we use all available information, including lexical, discourse, and contextual factors. Whereas the modular approach insists that syntactically based strategies are used first, with lexical and discourse factors coming in later, the interactive model asserts that we simultaneously use all available information to parse sentences.

subjective.question: Write a note on the constraint-based theory of parsing.
subjective.answer: Constraint-based theory, proposed by MacDonald, argues that all relevant information is available immediately to the parser during reading and listening. The incoming information is analysed and all possible constraints or outputs are activated and ranked according to the strength of the subsequent activation. The syntactic structure receiving the most support from the constraints will be highly activated and thus chosen. In essence, activated constraints are in competition with one another, and when two constraints are equally activated, ambiguity arises.

subjective.question: What is speech perception?
subjective.answer: Speech perception is a product of innate preparation (nature) and sensitivity to experience (nurture), as demonstrated in infants' abilities to perceive speech. Listeners must, in effect, categorize the sounds that they hear into one of the many classes of sounds that exist in their language. The task is extraordinarily complex for two major reasons: first, the environmental context often interferes with the speech signal — under normal listening conditions, the speech we hear competes with other stimuli, such as a conversation across the room, for our limited processing capacity.

subjective.question: Write a note on the motor theory of speech perception.
subjective.answer: The main rationale for the motor theory is that it deals effectively with the lack of invariance: it argues that although the relationship between acoustic structure and perception is quite complex, sounds are produced in similar ways but with varying acoustic representations, and are perceived in similar ways. The phonetic module, which links these perceptual and productive skills, may be an important innate mechanism in the acquisition of language, since infants can hear certain phonetic distinctions well before they are able to produce them. The theory makes testable claims about the brain mechanisms underlying language, and evidence (e.g. Ojemann) supports the idea that the perception and production areas of the brain are closely related.

subjective.question: Write a note on the feature level, word level and letter level of processing.
subjective.answer: At the feature level, the stimulus is represented in terms of the physical features that comprise a letter of the alphabet; for instance, the letter K may be represented as a vertical line and two diagonal lines. At the letter level, the visual stimulus is represented more abstractly as an identity separate from its physical manifestation — a stimulus may be represented as an F regardless of whether it is typewritten or handwritten. Finally, at the word level, an array of features and letters is recognized as a familiar word, and as the word is recognized, various properties of the word, such as its spelling, pronunciation and meaning, become available to us.

subjective.question: Write a note on story grammar in narrative discourse processing.
subjective.answer: Some of Bartlett's ideas have been formalized by contemporary researchers into the concept of a story grammar. A story grammar is a schema in semantic memory that identifies the typical or expected arrangement of events in a story. In general, story grammars view narratives as consisting of a setting, one or more episodes, and then an ending. In turn, episodes have a characteristic structure: some initiating event occurs, leading to an internal response on the part of the protagonist; the response leads to a goal, an attempt to reach the goal, and an outcome.

subjective.question: What is cohesion? Describe one type of cohesion.
subjective.answer: Cohesion refers to the links that hold a discourse together. One type of cohesion is called reference. Reference deals with the links between words and objects or events in the world; in discourse, it deals with the links between words (or phrases) and other words (or phrases) in the discourse. More precisely, reference is a semantic relation whereby information needed for the interpretation of one item is found elsewhere in the text. We often use pronouns such as she, he, it, his, her, and their to refer to earlier items.

subjective.question: What is local discourse structure? How do we build global structure?
subjective.answer: Comprehension of connected discourse depends less on the meanings of the individual sentences (local structure) than on their arrangement; it is entirely possible for a group of meaningful sentences to be thrown together in a way that makes no sense at all. To build global structure, we need to identify the important points of a passage even when they are not explicitly marked: as we become more familiar with the content and structure of an author's prose, we can gradually deduce the author's schema, selecting specific propositions as the most important ones and generalizing individual propositions into broader thematic statements.

subjective.question: Explain turn-taking in conversation.
subjective.answer: Turn-taking has been described as a process which obtains a distribution of talk across two participants. The time gap between one person stopping and the other starting is just a few fractions of a second, yet the co-ordination is achieved with some rapidity and turns are appropriated in an orderly fashion.

subjective.question: Write a note on closing a conversation.
subjective.answer: Conventions are at work when we close conversations. Schegloff and Sacks (1973) suggest that one way to end a conversation is to present a preclosing statement like 'we-ell', 'so-o-o', or 'OK', which signals a readiness to end the conversation. The listener may then accept the statement with an utterance such as 'yeah' or 'OK'; alternatively, the listener might bring up another topic and the conversation would continue.

subjective.question: How do friends and acquaintances differ with respect to conversation?
subjective.answer: One helpful concept here is what Clark calls common ground, which refers to the shared understanding of those involved in the conversation. For knowledge to qualify as common ground, person A must know a given information X, person B must know X, A must know that B knows, and B must know that A knows, and so on — both parties are aware that they share the information. Some common ground is culturally based, such as cultural values, commonly held beliefs, or culturally prescribed roles; other common ground is personal, built from shared experiences, and it is this personal common ground that differs between friends and mere acquaintances.

subjective.question: Explain identifying participants and nonparticipants in a conversation.
subjective.answer: During conversations, speakers establish their own and others' participant roles — who participates in the conversation and in what capacity. Conversations often take place in a context in which various types of nonparticipants are also present. We resort to a variety of strategies when dealing with overhearers, including disclosure, concealment, and indifference, and in private conversations we use strategies to conceal our meaning from eavesdroppers, such as referring to personal events ('the event we talked about yesterday'). While these roles might be fixed in some social settings (e.g. lectures), most conversational settings allow for shifting of roles.

subjective.question: Write a note on therapeutic discourse.
subjective.answer: Psychotherapists and related professionals attempt to help clients by listening to their concerns and talking to them; when the primary means of achieving therapeutic results is through language, therapists are especially skilled at conversational processes. We may distinguish three main tasks during therapy: first, the therapist listens carefully as the client reports experiences, issues, and concerns; second, the therapist interprets the client's experiences and symptoms; third, the therapist collaborates with the client regarding potential courses of action. These tasks are not necessarily organized sequentially; therapeutic sessions interweave data, interpretation, and suggestion in a complex pattern.

subjective.question: Write the types of figurative language.
subjective.answer: Figurative language is language that means one thing literally but is taken to mean something different. Its main types include: indirect speech acts, in which the speaker's intended meaning differs from the literal utterance, and metaphor — for example, when someone says 'Jim's head is full of rocks', we instantly recognize it as a metaphoric statement. Metaphors are a ubiquitous feature of language; for example, 'Billboards are warts on the landscape.'

subjective.question: Explain the pragmatic theory by Grice.
subjective.answer: It is generally held that linguistic communication takes place within a context of shared assumptions about communication. These implicit assumptions are referred to as conventions. Grice has identified four conventions (which he calls 'maxims') governing conversation: according to Grice, we strive to be informative, clear, relevant, and truthful. These conventions provide a basis for interpreting what others mean, because we generally assume, unless we have information to the contrary, that such conventions will be observed.

subjective.question: Define slips of the tongue and explain their types.
subjective.answer: Slips of the tongue are speech errors in which intended utterances are rearranged between other words or sounds. According to Gary Dell, they are significant because they show a person's widespread knowledge about language, including its sounds, structures, and meanings. There are three types: (1) Sound errors, in which the sounds in words close by are exchanged — instead of saying 'flower pot', one says 'power flot'; (2) Morpheme errors, in which morphemes (the smallest meaningful units in language) are switched — instead of 'self-destruct instruction', one says 'self-instruct destruction'; (3) Word errors, in which actual words are rearranged — instead of 'reading a book to my dog', one says 'reading a dog to my book'. Errors in speech production and perception are also called performance errors.

subjective.question: Write the common properties of speech errors.
subjective.answer: Garrett has identified generalizations about speech errors that reappear with striking regularity. First, elements that interact with one another tend to come from similar linguistic environments: the phonetic segments in the beginning of a word tend to be exchanged with other initial segments, and the same is true for middle and final segments — e.g. 'Children interfere with your nife lite' (night life). Second, elements that interact with one another tend to be similar to one another: consonants are invariably exchanged or shifted with other consonants but not with vowels, as in 'Sesame Street crackers' (sesame seed crackers).

subjective.question: What is the role of agreement in linguistic planning?
subjective.answer: In English, in order for a sentence to be grammatical there needs to be number agreement between subjects and either verbs or pronouns: we say 'The concerts this summer have been wonderful', not 'has been wonderful'. We sometimes make agreement errors that are instructive: in 'The time for fun and games is over', the head noun (time) controls the correct form of the subsequent verb (is), but we sometimes err by using a form (are) that matches the immediately preceding word (games). Such errors are helpful in evaluating serial and parallel models of production.

subjective.question: Differentiate between serial and parallel models of linguistic planning.
subjective.answer: Serial models assume that we begin with the overall idea of an utterance, followed by syntactic organization, content words, morphemes, and phonology; slips of the tongue typically involve just one level of planning, with other levels unaffected. Parallel models, by contrast, assume that the linguistic message is organized simultaneously at semantic, syntactic, morphological, and phonological levels: activation of a node at one level may trigger activation of nodes at other levels, and feedback may occur from morphological and phonological levels back to higher levels of processing. Models organized along these lines account for several important research findings.

subjective.question: Define self-monitoring.
subjective.answer: Speakers routinely monitor their utterances to ensure that they are saying what they wanted to say and in the way they wanted to say it. When errors are detected, speakers interrupt their speech nearly immediately and begin editing their utterance. Both the use of editing expressions and the linguistic structure of the repair itself appear to facilitate listener comprehension.

subjective.question: Explain the editing processes that intervene between the planning of an utterance and its articulation.
subjective.answer: In addition to the stages of planning, evidence indicates that editing processes intervene between the planning of an utterance and its articulation. These editing operations provide a last check to determine whether the planned utterance is linguistically and socially acceptable. Some monitoring and editing processes clearly occur after a speech segment is uttered — we often spontaneously correct ourselves — but there are also editing processes prior to articulation.

subjective.question: Explain 'editing expressions' briefly.
subjective.answer: The editing expression conveys to the listener the kind of trouble that the speaker is correcting. James (1972) analyzed utterances containing expressions such as 'uh' and 'oh', suggesting that these convey different meanings: in 'I saw ... uh ... 12 people at the party', the uh suggests that the speaker paused to try to remember the exact number of people, whereas 'I saw ... oh ... 12 people at the party' would be used when the speaker did not know the precise number but was trying to choose a number that was approximately correct.

subjective.question: Explain the tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) phenomenon.
subjective.answer: The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon occurs when we are not quite successful at retrieving a particular word but can remember something about how it sounds. William James described it as a gap in consciousness that is 'intensely active' — a sort of wraith of the name beckons us in a given direction, and if wrong names are proposed, the gap immediately negates them because they do not fit its mould. The TOT phenomenon was systematically studied for the first time by Brown and McNeill, who presented definitions of infrequent words, such as sextant, and asked subjects to produce the defined word; subjects in the TOT state retrieved but rejected similar-sounding words such as secant. Thus, we sometimes activate words by their sounds.

subjective.question: How do agrammatic patients process words?
subjective.answer: Agrammatic patients frequently omit closed-class words (and inflectional endings) from their sentences while preserving open-class words somewhat better. In addition, they process closed-class words differently than individuals without neurological damage.

subjective.topic: Language Development, Bilingualism and Sign Language
subjective.question: Define prelinguistic communication.
subjective.answer: Until the early part of their second year, infants communicate with their world primarily in nonverbal ways: they tug at people's clothes, point at desired objects, and wave bye-bye. These gestures, though basic, reveal a good deal about the infant's understanding of how communication works. It appears that the emergence of these communication skills is made possible by advances in the child's understanding of how actions can be used as means for achieving desired goals; these advances take place in the first year of life, suggesting that infants' understanding of communication precedes and facilitates much of the child's acquisition of phonology, syntax, and semantics.

subjective.topic: Language Development, Bilingualism and Sign Language
subjective.question: What is the Critical Period Hypothesis?
subjective.answer: The critical period hypothesis states that there is a period early in life in which we are especially prepared to acquire a language. Many investigators who favor the hypothesis suggest that there are neurological changes in the brain that leave a learner less able to acquire a language, although the nature of these supposed changes is not well understood; most commonly, these changes are assumed to occur near puberty. A landmark study was reported by Johnson and Newport (1989), who examined native speakers of Korean and Chinese who had immigrated to the United States at various ages between 3 and 39 years; on average, participants who arrived earlier (before puberty) performed better than those who arrived later.

subjective.topic: Language Development, Bilingualism and Sign Language
subjective.question: How do critical period effects influence second language learning?
subjective.answer: The evidence from second-language acquisition research has not provided unequivocal evidence for the critical period hypothesis. The best we can say is that young children generally learn a second language better than older children and adults, at least in the long run. Moreover, the advantage that younger learners display in some studies may be due to biological changes (as assumed by the critical period hypothesis), environmental factors, cognitive changes, or some combination of these factors.

subjective.topic: Language Development, Bilingualism and Sign Language
subjective.question: Who are feral or isolated children? Give an example.
subjective.answer: Feral children are those who have grown up in the wild, away from civilisation. Lane presented a detailed description of a boy named Victor, the 'Wild Boy of Aveyron', who was found in the woods of France in 1797, running naked through the woods searching for potatoes and nuts. At the time of his capture Victor was thought to be about 12 or 13 years old; he had no speech, although his hearing was normal. The physician Jean-Marc-Gaspard Itard worked intensively with Victor for five years, using techniques of language training and behavior modification similar to those used by modern researchers.

subjective.topic: Language Development, Bilingualism and Sign Language
subjective.question: Differentiate between simultaneous and sequential bilingualism.
subjective.answer: A distinction is drawn between simultaneous bilingualism and sequential bilingualism. When children acquire two languages at the same time, their bilingualism is referred to as simultaneous bilingualism; this most commonly happens when children are born into a bilingual community. Sequential bilingualism occurs when an individual (child or adult) acquires a second language after already acquiring a native language; this type is also referred to as second-language acquisition.

subjective.topic: Language Development, Bilingualism and Sign Language
subjective.question: What is cognitive control in bilingualism?
subjective.answer: Cognitive control is the ability to selectively attend to some stimuli and ignore others. A report by Bialystok, Craik, Klein, and Viswanathan (2004) suggests that bilingualism may help to offset age-related losses in cognitive or executive control. Using the Simon task — in which colored stimuli appear on the left or right of a screen and each color is associated with a response key on one side — they found that individuals are generally faster on congruent trials (stimulus and key on the same side) than on incongruent trials, and that bilinguals manage this conflict better.

subjective.topic: Language Development, Bilingualism and Sign Language
subjective.question: How can a child's multiword utterances be interpreted?
subjective.answer: Several different possibilities have been explored. A simple utterance such as 'baby cry' can be described in syntactic terms as a subject followed by a predicate; alternatively, in semantic terms as an agent (an animate being who is the instigator of an action) and an action; or in positional terms, with baby as a word typically in the initial position and cry as typically in the latter position. These characterizations differ in degree of abstractness, with the syntactic description as most abstract and the positional description as least abstract; the syntactic description does not appear to fit children's utterances, at least in the earliest stages.

subjective.topic: Language Development, Bilingualism and Sign Language
subjective.question: Write a note on sign language and American Sign Language (ASL).
subjective.answer: Sign languages are languages that use the visual-manual modality to convey meaning; they are expressed through manual articulations in combination with non-manual elements. Sign languages are full-fledged natural languages with their own grammar and lexicon; they are not universal and are not mutually intelligible with each other, although there are striking similarities among them. American Sign Language has its own set of grammatical rules and is a language independent of English; its grammatical organization shows striking similarities to spoken languages, suggesting that some basic concepts of language might be universal.

subjective.topic: Language Development, Bilingualism and Sign Language
subjective.question: Write a note on gender differences in conversation.
subjective.answer: Early studies of gender differences found that men interrupt women more than vice versa, a result that has not been found as often recently. Studies of conversational participants flesh out an outline of conversational processes while, at the same time, suggesting new avenues for research and theory.
